messages.content: I want to develop causal speech enhancement that distinguishes whispered consonants from transient noise without fabricating speech during ambiguous acoustic events. It should improve SI-SDR by at least 3 dB over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. Under matched phonetic evaluation, consonant deletion and insertion rates must not exceed the rates for the unprocessed inputs.

That sets two simultaneous requirements. The enhancement must produce an SI-SDR gain of at least 3 dB relative to the noisy inputs on the specified held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. It must also avoid worsening either consonant deletion or consonant insertion relative to unprocessed inputs when evaluated under matched phonetic conditions. The central difficulty is preserving genuine whispered consonants while not turning a brief, uncertain sound into speech that was not there.
What does causal add to that goal?

Causal means the enhancement cannot rely on audio that has not yet arrived when it processes the current audio. It still has to make the distinction between whispered consonants and transient noise, including ambiguous events, with that constraint. Causality describes what information is available to the enhancer; it does not by itself guarantee that consonants will be preserved or that speech will not be fabricated.
Why call out whispered consonants rather than just saying whispered speech?

The goal singles out the distinction between whispered consonants and transient noise. A short acoustic event might be important speech content, or it might be noise. Treating genuine whispered consonants as noise risks deletion; treating noise as a consonant risks insertion or fabricated speech. The requirement therefore concerns not just whether the output is cleaner, but whether it preserves the phonetic content represented by those events.
Does “without fabricating speech” mean the output must never contain a sound that is hard to classify?

No. An ambiguous event can remain difficult to classify. The stated concern is that enhancement must not create speech during such an event when the speech is not supported by the input. That is different from demanding that every uncertain sound be removed, or that every uncertainty be resolved with certainty.
Could the system meet the goal by removing every brief, noise-like event?

Not if that removes genuine whispered consonants and raises the consonant deletion rate above the unprocessed-input rate under matched phonetic evaluation. Suppressing transient noise is useful only within the full set of requirements; blanket suppression would not satisfy the goal merely because it makes the output sound quieter or cleaner.
What if it keeps or strengthens every brief event so it does not delete a consonant?

That would pose the opposite risk: noise could be represented as consonant content, raising the insertion rate or fabricating speech during an ambiguous event. The deletion and insertion limits apply separately. A lower deletion rate does not compensate for an insertion rate that exceeds its unprocessed-input counterpart.
Can you put the SI-SDR target in plain terms?

The enhanced output must score at least 3 dB higher in SI-SDR than the noisy input on the specified held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. It is a required improvement over the noisy-input comparison, not a requirement that SI-SDR merely reach an absolute value of 3 dB. The goal does not specify a finer breakdown of that gain across individual recordings.
And the phonetic limits use a different comparison?

They use the unprocessed inputs as the reference for the rates: the enhanced output’s consonant deletion rate must be no higher than the unprocessed-input deletion rate, and its consonant insertion rate must be no higher than the unprocessed-input insertion rate. Those comparisons are to be made under matched phonetic evaluation. The SI-SDR gain does not waive either phonetic limit.
Why specify matched phonetic evaluation?

It makes the rate comparisons like-for-like. If the enhanced output and unprocessed input were assessed under different phonetic evaluation conditions, a difference in deletion or insertion rates might not reflect the enhancement itself. The requirement names matched evaluation but does not prescribe a particular evaluation procedure here.
Suppose SI-SDR improves enough, but consonant deletion gets worse while insertion stays the same. Would that meet the requirements?

No. Even with an SI-SDR improvement of at least 3 dB and no increase in insertion, a deletion rate above the unprocessed-input rate would violate the deletion limit. Both phonetic rates have to remain at or below their respective unprocessed-input rates.
What if both phonetic rates are acceptable but the SI-SDR gain is less than 3 dB?

That would also fall short. Protecting consonants and avoiding fabricated speech are necessary, but the stated objective additionally requires an SI-SDR improvement of at least 3 dB over the noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises.
Is the phrase “unseen noises” interchangeable with “held-out whispered speech”?

They identify different parts of the stated evaluation conditions: the speech is held-out whispered speech, and the noises are unseen. Both matter to the SI-SDR requirement. Neither phrase alone replaces the full condition.
So a cleaner signal is not automatically a better result here?

Correct. A result that improves SI-SDR but deletes more consonants or inserts more consonants than the unprocessed input under matched phonetic evaluation would not meet the stated requirements. The intended enhancement has to improve the signal measure while respecting both phonetic limits and avoiding fabricated speech in ambiguous acoustic events.
Can we state the whole objective compactly without losing those distinctions?

Develop causal speech enhancement that distinguishes whispered consonants from transient noise without fabricating speech during ambiguous acoustic events. On held-out whispered speech and unseen noises, require an SI-SDR improvement of at least 3 dB over noisy inputs. Under matched phonetic evaluation, require both consonant deletion and consonant insertion rates to be no higher than their respective unprocessed-input rates.
How would you approach the causal enhancement goal without forcing a decision on every ambiguous short sound?

I would propose training a causal, 160-ms-context bounded-mask estimator with transient-versus-consonant supervision, an uncertainty-gated input bypass, and consonant insertion and deletion penalties. The supervision is intended to help distinguish transient noise from whispered consonants. The bypass gives the estimator a way to defer to the input when its decision is uncertain, while the penalties make both kinds of consonant error relevant during training. This is a proposed approach, not an established result.
What does the 160-ms context specify?

It specifies the context length for the proposed causal estimator: 160 ms. Because the estimator is causal, processing the current audio cannot depend on future audio. The proposal does not specify further details about how that available context is represented or used.
Does causal mean it has to decide from a single instant of sound?

No. The proposed estimator has 160 ms of context, so it need not treat an instant in isolation. Causality limits it to information available by the time it processes the current audio; it does not eliminate the stated context.
Why use a bounded-mask estimator?

A mask estimator is a way to produce an enhanced signal by controlling what is retained from the input, and 'bounded' says the proposed mask is subject to limits. That fits an approach intended to avoid unconstrained alteration of ambiguous events. The proposal does not give numerical mask bounds or claim that bounding the mask alone prevents fabricated speech.
Would the bounded mask necessarily leave every whispered consonant untouched?

No. A bound on the mask is not, by itself, a guarantee that a genuine consonant will be preserved. The proposed transient-versus-consonant supervision and consonant deletion penalty address that risk, but whether the complete approach satisfies the phonetic requirement would still have to be evaluated.
What is transient-versus-consonant supervision meant to contribute?

It directs training toward the distinction at the center of the task: a brief event can be transient noise or a whispered consonant. The intent is to make that distinction matter explicitly to the estimator rather than treating all short events alike. The proposal does not specify the form of the supervision or say that every ambiguous event can be classified reliably.
If an event remains ambiguous, what is the uncertainty-gated input bypass for?

The proposed bypass provides a way for uncertainty to favor the input rather than an enhancement decision that might erase a consonant or introduce speech-like content. 'Uncertainty-gated' indicates that uncertainty controls whether the input bypass is used. The proposal does not specify an uncertainty measure, a threshold, or the precise behavior of the gate.
Is bypassing the input the same thing as deciding that the event is a consonant?

No. Passing through the input would not establish whether the event is speech or noise. Its role in this proposal is to avoid forcing a potentially harmful enhancement decision when the distinction is uncertain. It is a fallback, not a phonetic classification or a guarantee of a correct output.
Why include separate insertion and deletion penalties?

They address different failure modes. A deletion penalty discourages losing genuine consonants; an insertion penalty discourages introducing consonant content that was not present. Training only against one kind of error could still leave the other kind unaddressed. Including both reflects the requirement that neither consonant deletion nor consonant insertion worsen relative to the unprocessed input under matched phonetic evaluation.
Do those training penalties ensure the evaluated rates will stay at or below the unprocessed-input rates?

No. Penalties express what the training should discourage; they do not establish the resulting rates. The enhanced output would still need matched phonetic evaluation against the unprocessed input for both deletion and insertion. The proposal contains no measured rates or claim that either limit has been met.
Could the SI-SDR target be treated as enough evidence that the transient-versus-consonant distinction worked?

No. An SI-SDR improvement of at least 3 dB over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises is one requirement, but it would not on its own show that consonant deletion and insertion stayed within their respective limits. The proposed supervision, bypass, and penalties are intended to address those phonetic risks; their effectiveness remains to be tested.
Does the proposal specify how the mask, bypass, and penalties are combined mathematically?

It does not. It identifies the proposed components and their roles, but gives no mask bounds, gating rule, penalty weights, or exact training objective. Those details should not be assumed from the component names.
Then what is the central idea tying the components together?

Use a causal estimator with 160 ms of context to enhance the signal, explicitly train it on the transient-versus-consonant distinction, and avoid overcommitting on uncertain events through an input bypass. Bound the mask and penalize both consonant insertions and deletions so that suppressing noise does not become the only consideration. The combination is a proposal for pursuing the speech-enhancement goal, not evidence that it has achieved it.
Can transient-supervised gating preserve weak whispered /s/ without mistaking unseen clicks for consonants under 160-ms causal context?

That is the key unresolved question for the proposed approach. Transient-versus-consonant supervision could help the gate distinguish those events, and an uncertainty-gated input bypass could keep it from forcing a decision when evidence is weak. But neither feature establishes that a weak whispered /s/ will be preserved or that an unseen click will not be mistaken for a consonant, especially when decisions are limited to causal 160-ms context.
Why is weak whispered /s/ a particularly useful way to pose the question?

It makes the preservation side concrete. If the enhancer treats a genuine but weak /s/ as transient noise, it may suppress consonant content. The question pairs that risk with the opposite one: treating an unseen click as a consonant. A useful gate has to avoid both errors rather than improving one at the expense of the other.
Does transient-versus-consonant supervision tell the gate what to do with a weak /s/?

It supplies a training distinction relevant to that decision. It does not guarantee that the distinction will remain clear for every weak /s/, nor that it will generalize to unseen clicks. The question is whether the learned distinction is reliable in those cases, not merely whether the supervision names the right categories.
Could the gate simply favor keeping anything that might be /s/?

That might reduce the risk of removing a weak /s/, but it could also retain or treat clicks as consonant content. Favoring preservation indiscriminately does not resolve the question’s second half. The gate would need to handle uncertainty without equating every ambiguous transient with speech.
Then could it favor rejecting anything that might be a click?

That creates the reverse risk: a weak whispered /s/ might be rejected along with the clicks. The question is about maintaining the distinction under limited causal context, not finding a rule that protects only one side of it.
How does the input bypass affect those two risks?

When uncertainty triggers the proposed bypass, the input can pass through instead of being subjected to a more decisive enhancement action. That may help avoid suppressing a genuine /s/ or transforming an ambiguous event into consonant-like output. But passing through an event does not establish whether it is /s/ or a click, and it does not necessarily remove an unseen click. The bypass is a way to limit an uncertain intervention, not a solution to the classification question by itself.
If a click passes through unchanged, is that the same as mistaking it for a consonant?

Not necessarily. Passing through an input event and classifying or enhancing it as consonant content are different. A bypass could leave a click audible without fabricating a consonant from it. Whether the output produces a consonant insertion is a separate phonetic question; the mere presence of the original click does not answer it.
What does the 160-ms causal context contribute to the uncertainty?

The gate can use the proposed 160 ms of context, but it cannot consult future audio when making a current decision. Available context may help interpret an event, yet the stated context limit does not guarantee that a weak /s/ and an unseen click will be distinguishable in every case. The question asks whether the proposed gating remains effective under that constraint.
Does the question imply that 160 ms is too short?

No. It identifies 160-ms causal context as the condition under which the distinction must be made. It does not state that the context is sufficient or insufficient. Either conclusion would require evidence not supplied by the question.
Is the main uncertainty about the gate, or about the transient-versus-consonant supervision?

It concerns their combination. Supervision may shape what the estimator regards as consonant or transient noise; gating determines how uncertainty affects the output. Weak /s/ and unseen clicks probe whether those pieces work together without creating either excessive suppression or false consonant content. The question does not isolate one component as the cause of a possible failure.
Would a bounded mask settle the issue?

No. The proposed bounded mask constrains the estimator, but a constrained change can still remove part of a weak consonant or handle a click poorly. The bound alone does not show that the gate identifies uncertainty correctly or distinguishes these events under causal context.
And do consonant insertion and deletion penalties settle it?

They make both errors relevant during training, but they do not prove how the trained system behaves on weak whispered /s/ or unseen clicks. The penalties reflect the need to avoid deleting a real consonant and inserting one where there is none; the question remains whether the resulting behavior actually meets those aims.
Could we answer the question from an SI-SDR improvement alone?

No. An SI-SDR improvement would not, by itself, show that weak /s/ survived or that clicks were not mistaken for consonants. Those are phonetic distinctions. The goal also calls for at least a 3 dB SI-SDR improvement over noisy inputs on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises, while consonant deletion and insertion rates must each be no higher than their unprocessed-input rates under matched phonetic evaluation.
So what would a careful answer to the question sound like right now?

Transient-supervised gating with an uncertainty-gated bypass is intended to preserve uncertain genuine consonants without manufacturing consonant content from transient noise. Whether it can preserve weak whispered /s/ while avoiding consonant mistakes on unseen clicks within 160-ms causal context is not established here. The two possible errors must be considered separately; success at avoiding one would not demonstrate success at avoiding the other.

I want to make the possible answer more concrete: on unseen-click mixtures, bypass gating yields at least a 3 dB SI-SDR gain over the noisy input without increasing /s/ deletion or click-induced insertion. Can we frame that as a hypothesis?

Yes. As a hypothesis, it predicts three outcomes together on unseen-click mixtures: an SI-SDR gain of at least 3 dB over the noisy input, no increase in /s/ deletion, and no increase in click-induced insertion. It is not a report that any of those outcomes has been observed.
Why specify unseen-click mixtures instead of just saying noisy speech?

That wording focuses the hypothesis on mixtures containing clicks the system has not seen. The clicks matter because they present the transient-versus-consonant ambiguity in a concrete form. The hypothesis does not, by itself, assert the same outcome for every other kind of unseen noise.
Is the 3 dB part an absolute SI-SDR score?

No. It is a gain over the noisy input: the enhanced output’s SI-SDR would need to be at least 3 dB higher than the noisy input’s SI-SDR on those mixtures. The hypothesis does not specify an absolute output SI-SDR value.
What is the significance of saying “bypass gating yields” the gain?

It attributes the predicted behavior to the proposed bypass gating, rather than merely expressing a general wish for cleaner audio. But the wording remains hypothetical; it does not establish that the gating causes the gain or that its contribution has been isolated from the rest of the proposed enhancer.
Could the bypass be useful for /s/ preservation even if it sometimes leaves a click in the output?

Conceptually, yes. Bypassing an uncertain event could avoid suppressing a genuine /s/, while an input click might also remain audible. Leaving a click audible is not automatically the same as inserting a consonant because of that click. The hypothesis requires no increase in click-induced insertion as well as no increase in /s/ deletion; it does not say every click must disappear.
Then does “without increasing /s/ deletion” mean no /s/ can ever be deleted?

No. It means the /s/ deletion rate must not increase relative to the relevant comparison, not that deletion must be zero. In the goal’s matched phonetic evaluation, the unprocessed input provides the comparison for consonant deletion and insertion rates. The hypothesis specifically names /s/ deletion rather than claiming that all consonant deletions have been eliminated.
And what exactly is a click-induced insertion in this wording?

It is an insertion of consonant content associated with a click being mistaken for speech. The hypothesis says such insertions do not increase. It does not equate every audible click with an inserted consonant, and it does not claim that no insertion of any kind can occur.
Could a large SI-SDR gain make up for an increase in click-induced insertion?

Not under this hypothesis. The gain and the two phonetic conditions are simultaneous predictions. Even if SI-SDR improved by at least 3 dB over the noisy input, an increase in click-induced insertion would contradict the stated hypothesis.
What if /s/ deletion stays level and click-induced insertion stays level, but the SI-SDR gain is only 2 dB?
That would not satisfy the hypothesis either. Holding those errors steady addresses its phonetic conditions, but 2 dB is below the stated threshold of at least 3 dB over the noisy input.
Does this hypothesis answer the entire speech-enhancement goal?

It addresses a focused case: unseen-click mixtures, with particular attention to /s/ deletion and click-induced insertion. The broader goal concerns held-out whispered speech and unseen noises, an SI-SDR improvement of at least 3 dB over noisy inputs, and consonant deletion and insertion rates that do not exceed unprocessed-input rates under matched phonetic evaluation. The focused hypothesis should not be read as a claim that the broader requirements have already been met.
Is the causal 160-ms context still relevant, even though the hypothesis does not repeat it?

Yes, as context for the proposed bypass gating being discussed: it belongs to the causal, 160-ms-context estimator. The hypothesis asks whether that proposed approach can produce the stated outcomes on unseen-click mixtures. It does not provide a separate finding about how much the 160-ms context contributes.
Would no increase in /s/ deletion alone show that weak whispered /s/ was handled well?

It would support the preservation side of this focused prediction, but not the whole prediction. Click-induced insertion could still increase, or SI-SDR gain could fall below 3 dB. The hypothesis deliberately pairs /s/ preservation with avoiding consonant mistakes from unseen clicks and achieving the signal-level gain.
So the cautious way to say it is that we expect all three, but we do not yet know whether they occur together?

Exactly. The hypothesis is that bypass gating yields at least a 3 dB SI-SDR gain over noisy input on unseen-click mixtures without increasing either /s/ deletion or click-induced insertion. It makes a testable prediction about those outcomes occurring together; it does not present them as established results.
To evaluate that hypothesis, I want to use WhisperClick-HO mixtures with unseen clicks and measure SI-SDR gain, matched /s/ deletions, and click-induced insertions versus noisy inputs.

That evaluation keeps the three predicted outcomes distinct. On the WhisperClick-HO mixtures with unseen clicks, measure the enhanced output’s SI-SDR gain over the noisy inputs. Under matched phonetic evaluation, compare /s/ deletions and click-induced insertions with those for the noisy inputs. The activity specifies what to measure; it does not report results.
What would the SI-SDR comparison tell us?

It would tell us whether enhancement improves SI-SDR relative to the noisy inputs on these mixtures, and whether the gain reaches the hypothesis’s threshold of at least 3 dB. It would not, on its own, tell us whether weak /s/ sounds were preserved or whether clicks led to consonant insertions.
Why measure /s/ deletions separately?

Because a signal-level improvement could coincide with losing genuine /s/ content. The matched /s/ deletion comparison asks specifically whether the enhanced output deletes more /s/ sounds than the noisy inputs. For the focused hypothesis, that rate must not increase.
And click-induced insertions address the other side of the ambiguity?

Yes. That measure asks whether unseen clicks lead to more inserted consonant content after enhancement than in the noisy inputs. It separates the risk of mistaking a click for a consonant from the risk of deleting a real /s/. A favorable /s/ deletion comparison would not substitute for the insertion comparison.
When you say “matched,” are all three measurements the same kind of measurement?

No. SI-SDR gain is a signal-level comparison with the noisy input. The /s/ deletions are assessed under matched phonetic evaluation, so the enhanced and noisy-input comparisons use like-for-like phonetic conditions. Click-induced insertions are also compared against the noisy inputs. These are complementary measurements, not interchangeable scores.
Does the activity require every click to be removed?

No. It calls for measuring click-induced insertions, not for treating every audible click as a failure. An input click remaining audible and an output being assessed as containing an inserted consonant because of a click are different matters. The stated comparison is whether click-induced insertions increase versus the noisy inputs.
If the enhancement keeps a weak /s/ but also makes a click seem like a consonant, how should we read that?

The /s/ preservation and click-induced insertion outcomes would have to be read separately. Preserving /s/ would not cancel out an increase in click-induced insertions. The hypothesis predicts no increase in either error while achieving the SI-SDR gain.
What if the insertion comparison is favorable but /s/ deletions rise?

Then the deletion part of the hypothesis would not hold, regardless of the insertion comparison. This evaluation is designed to expose that trade-off rather than letting one favorable measurement stand in for all three.
Should the SI-SDR gain be reported as the enhanced score alone?
No. The specified measure is SI-SDR gain over the noisy inputs. An enhanced-output score by itself would omit the comparison needed to determine whether the gain reaches at least 3 dB.
Does naming WhisperClick-HO tell us anything else about how those mixtures were made?

Not from this activity. It identifies the mixtures to evaluate and states that they contain unseen clicks, but it does not specify their construction or any additional properties. Those details should not be inferred from the name.
Can we say yet whether bypass gating passes this evaluation?

No. The evaluation activity names the measurements and their noisy-input comparisons; it supplies no measured SI-SDR gain, /s/ deletion result, or click-induced insertion result. Whether the outcomes jointly support the hypothesis remains an open empirical question.
What is the most important thing to keep straight when reading the eventual measurements?

Keep the three comparisons separate and apply the stated conditions to each: SI-SDR gain of at least 3 dB over noisy inputs on the WhisperClick-HO unseen-click mixtures, no increase in matched /s/ deletions versus noisy inputs, and no increase in click-induced insertions versus noisy inputs. None of those conclusions follows merely from performing the evaluation.
The WhisperClick-HO measurements are in: SI-SDR improved by 3.4 dB, /s/ deletions fell from 9.1% to 8.2%, and click-induced insertions fell from 2.5% to 2.0%.

On the evaluated WhisperClick-HO mixtures, that is a 3.4 dB SI-SDR improvement over the noisy inputs. In the matched phonetic comparison, /s/ deletions decreased by 0.9 percentage points, from 9.1% for the noisy inputs to 8.2% after enhancement. Click-induced insertions decreased by 0.5 percentage points, from 2.5% to 2.0%.
Are those last two changes percentage-point changes?

Yes. Subtracting 8.2% from 9.1% gives a decrease of 0.9 percentage points. Subtracting 2.0% from 2.5% gives a decrease of 0.5 percentage points. Calling them percentage-point changes keeps them distinct from relative percentage changes.
Can you spell out which number belongs to the noisy input in each comparison?

For /s/ deletions, 9.1% is the noisy-input rate and 8.2% is the enhanced-output rate. For click-induced insertions, 2.5% is the noisy-input rate and 2.0% is the enhanced-output rate. The SI-SDR figure is already expressed as a gain: the enhanced output improved by 3.4 dB over the noisy input.
Does 3.4 dB mean the enhanced output had an SI-SDR of 3.4 dB?
No. It describes the improvement relative to the noisy input, not the enhanced output’s absolute SI-SDR. The absolute SI-SDR values are not included in these reported measurements.
How should I describe the /s/ result without making it sound as if no /s/ was ever lost?
Say that the measured /s/ deletion rate fell from 9.1% on the noisy inputs to 8.2% after enhancement. That reports a lower rate while making clear that the enhanced-output rate was not zero.
And the click number does not mean all clicks disappeared, right?

Right. It is the rate of click-induced consonant insertions, not a count of audible clicks or a measure of click removal. The reported rate fell from 2.5% to 2.0%; it does not say that every click was removed or that no click-induced insertion occurred.
Is it fair to say the two phonetic measures moved in the same direction?

Yes. Both reported rates decreased on WhisperClick-HO: /s/ deletions from 9.1% to 8.2%, and click-induced insertions from 2.5% to 2.0%. They remain separate measures of different errors, even though both decreased.
Does the result identify how much of the SI-SDR change came specifically from the bypass gate?
No. The reported figure is the 3.4 dB SI-SDR improvement for the evaluated output. These measurements do not isolate a numerical contribution from the bypass gate or from any other component.
Could I describe the /s/ figures as a matched comparison?

Yes. The evaluation specified matched /s/ deletions versus noisy inputs, and the reported rates are 9.1% for noisy inputs and 8.2% after enhancement. Keeping that comparison explicit helps avoid presenting 8.2% as a standalone rate without its reference.
What is the scope of the evidence as stated?

These are measurements on WhisperClick-HO, the evaluated mixtures with unseen clicks. The reported quantities are the 3.4 dB SI-SDR improvement, the two /s/ deletion rates, and the two click-induced insertion rates. No results for other mixtures or other phonetic categories are given here.
Please give me a concise results sentence that keeps the baselines and units clear.

On WhisperClick-HO mixtures with unseen clicks, enhancement improved SI-SDR by 3.4 dB over noisy inputs; under the matched comparison, /s/ deletions fell from 9.1% to 8.2%, while click-induced insertions fell from 2.5% to 2.0%.
Given the WhisperClick-HO outcome, should we retain the uncertainty-gated bypass for click-like transients?

Yes. The decision is to retain the uncertainty-gated bypass for click-like transients. The stated reason is that WhisperClick-HO exceeded the SI-SDR target while reducing both /s/ deletions and click-induced insertions.
Does retaining it mean bypassing every click-like sound?
No. The decision retains an uncertainty-gated bypass for click-like transients; it does not say to bypass every such sound unconditionally. Uncertainty remains part of when the bypass is used.
Why do the /s/ deletions matter to a decision about clicks?

The enhancer needs to avoid mistaking a weak whispered /s/ for a transient and suppressing it. Reduced /s/ deletions address that preservation concern, while reduced click-induced insertions address the opposite concern of treating clicks as consonant content. Both reductions are part of the stated reason for retaining the bypass.
Would exceeding the SI-SDR target alone have been the reason stated here?

No. This decision explicitly rests on the combined WhisperClick-HO outcome: exceeding the SI-SDR target *and* reducing /s/ deletions and click-induced insertions. It does not present signal-level improvement as a substitute for the phonetic comparisons.
Does the decision prove that the bypass itself caused each improvement?

No. It gives the WhisperClick-HO outcome as the reason to retain the bypass, but it does not isolate the bypass’s causal contribution to each measured improvement. Retaining a component on that basis is narrower than claiming it independently caused all three outcomes.
Should I describe this as a decision about all transient noise?
Keep the scope to click-like transients. The decision does not say to retain the same behavior for every kind of transient noise, and the stated reason is specifically the WhisperClick-HO outcome.
Does retaining the bypass mean an ambiguous sound is declared to be speech?

No. The bypass is a way to avoid forcing an enhancement decision when uncertainty warrants it. Retaining it for click-like transients does not classify every ambiguous event as a consonant, nor does it mean every such event must be removed.
Can I say the WhisperClick-HO outcome supports keeping the bypass without claiming the entire enhancement goal is settled?

Yes. You can state the decision and its specific reason: retain the uncertainty-gated bypass for click-like transients because WhisperClick-HO exceeded the SI-SDR target while reducing /s/ deletions and click-induced insertions. That does not, by itself, declare outcomes for other noises or every consonant.

With the uncertainty-gated bypass retained, I want to train WhisperMix-v2 and then test held-out whispered speakers against unseen noises. The test should use SI-SDR and matched consonant deletion and insertion rates.

That is a plan for training and evaluation, not a report of a WhisperMix-v2 result. It keeps the retained bypass in the approach, then assesses performance on held-out whispered speakers against unseen noises using both SI-SDR and matched consonant deletion and insertion rates.
What does “with the retained bypass” commit us to in this plan?

It means the planned training of WhisperMix-v2 includes the uncertainty-gated bypass that was retained for click-like transients. It does not specify a new gating rule, say that every transient will be bypassed, or establish how the bypass will behave in the planned test.
Does the plan say WhisperMix-v2 has already been trained?
No. “Train WhisperMix-v2” is a proposed activity. The plan supplies neither a completed training outcome nor evaluation measurements.
Why specify held-out whispered speakers?

That identifies whom the planned test concerns: whispered speakers held out from training. It keeps the evaluation focused on whispered speech beyond the speakers used for training. The plan does not give a number of speakers or describe how they are selected.
And what is the distinct role of unseen noises?

They are the noise condition for the planned test. “Held-out whispered speakers” concerns the speakers, while “unseen noises” concerns the noises. Naming both avoids treating either condition as a substitute for the other.
Could I shorten that to “test on new audio”?

That would lose important conditions. The plan specifically calls for testing held-out whispered speakers against unseen noises. “New audio” would not preserve either the whispered-speaker condition or the unseen-noise condition.
What will SI-SDR tell us in that test?

It provides the signal-level measure for the planned evaluation. To assess the stated enhancement goal, its improvement would be compared with the noisy inputs, with a target of at least 3 dB on held-out whispered speech and unseen noises. The plan does not provide an SI-SDR value or predict what WhisperMix-v2 will achieve.
Why not just test SI-SDR and stop there?

SI-SDR alone would not show whether the enhancement preserves consonants or introduces consonant content. The plan therefore also calls for matched consonant deletion and insertion rates. The goal requires each of those rates to be no higher than its unprocessed-input rate under matched phonetic evaluation; an SI-SDR gain cannot replace either comparison.
Are deletion and insertion one combined error rate here?

No. They are two separate rates. Deletion concerns consonant content lost from the output; insertion concerns consonant content added where it should not be. The planned test needs both, because a favorable result for one would not establish a favorable result for the other.
What does “matched” change about how we interpret those rates?

It calls for like-for-like phonetic evaluation of the enhanced and unprocessed inputs. That matters when comparing consonant deletion rates and, separately, consonant insertion rates. The plan does not specify a particular scoring procedure beyond requiring matched comparisons.
Does this test focus only on /s/ and clicks?

No. The plan names consonant deletion and insertion rates, held-out whispered speakers, and unseen noises. It does not limit the planned phonetic evaluation to /s/ or the noise condition to clicks. It also does not specify a breakdown by individual consonant or noise type.
Can we assume what WhisperMix-v2 contains from its name?
No. The plan names WhisperMix-v2 as what will be trained, but does not describe its contents, construction, or training settings. Those details cannot be inferred from the name.
Does keeping the bypass guarantee that ambiguous events will not become fabricated speech on unseen noises?

No. Retaining the bypass is part of the planned approach, not a guarantee about its behavior in this test.
